title: Asia stocks slide as China chip threat hits Samsung, SK Hynix; oil retreats
full_text:
Wall Street kicks off key week of bank earnings and CPI data with a mixed session
Investing.com -- Asian stocks fell sharply on Tuesday as a selloff in technology shares spread from Wall Street, with concerns over Chinese semiconductor competition and the returns on artificial-intelligence investments triggering heavy losses in South Korea and Taiwan.
Oil prices eased but remained elevated amid escalating Middle East tensions, while investors braced for U.S. inflation data and the start of a busy corporate earnings season.
The MSCI AC Asia Pacific fell around 2%, putting it on track for its weakest close since August. South Korea’s KOSPI plunged 7.2% to 5,923.37, its lowest level since July, while Japan’s Nikkei 225 dropped 2.7% to 67,200.5 after returning from a long weekend.
Wall Street’s technology selloff set the tone. The Nasdaq Composite fell 0.5% on Monday as semiconductor stocks weakened, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index sank 2.7% to its lowest level since mid-September. In Asian trade, Nasdaq 100 futures fell 0.8%, while S&P 500 futures lost 0.2%.
Brent crude slipped about 1.1% to around $105.50 a barrel, trimming its recent advance but remaining near a two-week high.
Korean chipmakers plunge as CXMT raises competitive threat
South Korean memory-chip makers bore the brunt of the selloff. SK Hynix fell 8.9%, while Samsung Electronics dropped 8%. LG Innotek slid 8.9%.
The selloff followed reports that China’s CXMT is advancing a higher-density 4F² DRAM design, with next-generation server-memory products targeted for year-end, raising competition concerns for established chipmakers. CXMT shares fell 2.4%.
The technology selloff extended across the regional supply chain. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing fell 1.6%, Foxconn lost 2.1% and Largan slipped 0.6%. In Japan, Kioxia plunged 12.4%, TDK dropped 6.2% and Murata Manufacturing fell 6.9%.
High financing costs and stretched valuations are fueling doubts over AI spending returns, leaving technology stocks vulnerable to earnings disappointments after the S&P 500’s nearly 120% rally from its 2022 low.
Broadcom Chief Executive Hock Tan added to investor caution on Monday, warning that some participants in the AI boom were taking positions without fully understanding the businesses or technology behind them.
Anna Wu, investment strategist and founder of Floodlines Research, said the semiconductor sector had become especially sensitive to any sign of disappointment after its strong gains.
She noted that, across 14 major AI companies, 23 of 42 earnings reports this year had beaten forecasts without winning a positive market reaction. In the latest reporting season, six of the 14 companies that beat estimates were still sold or ignored, compared with seven and 10 in the first two seasons, respectively.
Oil, inflation and earnings keep investors cautious
Brent crude traded around $105.50 a barrel as investors weighed Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia against the prospect of increased Russian diesel supplies.
Iran-backed Houthi forces struck Riyadh’s main airport over the weekend, raising fears of wider conflict, while Trump’s claim of a Russia-Ukraine energy truce remained unconfirmed and his proposal for Russia to boost diesel exports drew bipartisan legal concerns.
Investors are now looking to Wednesday’s U.S. consumer price index report for clues on the Federal Reserve’s next move. Producer prices and retail sales are also due later in the week. Any upside surprise in inflation could revive expectations of tighter policy and renew pressure on long-term yields.
Japan’s producer-price inflation eased to 6.8% in September from 7.6% in August, below forecasts, but a 24.5% jump in yen-based import prices amid currency weakness and higher raw-material costs could keep pressure on the BOJ to tighten policy at its October 29-30 meeting.
The RBA’s September minutes showed a unanimous 25-basis-point rate hike to 4.60%, driven by energy prices, AI-related demand and capacity constraints, despite slowing output growth, weaker household spending and gradually easing labour-market conditions.
Meanwhile, third-quarter earnings from major U.S. banks begin Tuesday, with JPMorgan Chase, Goldman Sachs, Citigroup and Wells Fargo due to report. Bank of America and Morgan Stanley follow on Wednesday.

Higher borrowing costs typically weigh on gold because the non-yielding metal becomes less attractive relative to interest-bearing assets. Persistent inflation and heavy government borrowing have also kept interest rates and bond yields elevated, further limiting bullion’s appeal.

title: AI investment props up global growth, but war and debt threaten outlook, IMF says
full_text:
Wall Street kicks off key week of bank earnings and CPI data with a mixed session
By David Lawder
BANGKOK, Oct 13 (Reuters) - The global economy will still manage to top 3% real GDP growth this year as strong AI investment offsets the energy shock from the war in the Middle East, but downside risks are mounting and more countries are being left behind and vulnerable to rising debt loads, the International Monetary Fund said on Tuesday.
Despite a more protracted conflict that has kept oil prices above $100 a barrel, the IMF is forecasting 2026 global growth at 3.1%, a slight uptick from the 3.0% it predicted in July.
The World Economic Outlook forecast, released as global economic and finance leaders gather in Bangkok for the IMF and World Bank annual meetings, is about even with the most optimistic scenario issued in April but below 2025 global growth of 3.5%.
For 2027, the IMF predicts 3.4% global growth, flat with the July forecast and up 0.2 percentage point from April.
The slight improvement is largely due to continued strong investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure, prompting growth upgrades for key advanced economies building AI platforms and especially for countries supplying AI hardware, including South Korea, Malaysia, Mexico and Thailand, which is hosting the meetings this week.
"The global economy has been resilient, but that resilience is reaching its limits, so we need to move from just coping to rebuilding," the IMF’s chief economist, Silvana Tenreyro, told a news conference. "We need to restore fiscal space. We need to rebuild supply-side resilience."
She said major downside risks to growth include a prolonged, intensified war in the Middle East that spikes inflation pressures, rising bond yields that raise government borrowing costs, El Nino-driven extreme weather events and a reassessment of AI profitability that craters investment and asset prices.
Countries and companies moved quickly to mitigate the oil price shock, drawing down reserves, substituting other suppliers and energy sources and cutting oil demand, Petya Koeva Brooks, the IMF’s deputy research director, told Reuters in a separate interview. She said global growth would have fallen to 2.5% this year without these measures, but their effect is fading as the war drags on.
The IMF noted a growing divergence between countries benefiting from AI and those bypassed by it. Just 32 countries now account for 95% of global growth, compared to 54 countries in April.
Downward growth revisions have become more widespread, with the IMF downgrading 47% of economies since the April forecasts were issued, including several energy importers outside AI value chains.
Hardest hit by downgrades were the Gulf countries directly impacted by the US-Israeli war against Iran, with Saudi Arabia’s GDP now forecast to contract 3.3% this year compared with the 1.7% growth predicted in July.
Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates are also expected to fall into deep recessions, with 2026 contractions of 7.6%, 16%, 16.7%, 15.6% and 3.9%, respectively.
UNITED STATES FLAT, IMPROVEMENT IN EUROPE
Among major economies, the IMF forecast US growth of 2.3% for both 2026 and 2027, unchanged for this year and 0.1 percentage point higher for next year. The US economy is expected to be supported by robust private consumption, tax cuts and AI investment, though the boost from AI will be offset by its large import content.
Euro zone growth for 2026 was upgraded to 1.1% from 0.9% in July due to stronger investment in AI, participation in AI value chains such as chemical production in Germany, and higher defense spending in EU countries. Britain’s 2026 growth forecast also was upgraded by 0.3 percentage point from July to 1.3% due to larger AI investment.
The IMF forecast China’s growth at 4.5% for 2026 and 4.0% for 2027, both down 0.1 percentage point from July, as higher oil prices exacerbate weak domestic demand despite strong exports.
India remains the world’s fastest-growing major economy at 7.0% for both 2026 and 2027, up 0.6 percentage point this year and 0.3 percentage point next year compared with the July forecasts amid robust domestic demand, services activity and AI investment.
The AI investment surge is projected to keep upward pressure on prices, with global headline consumer price inflation forecast at 4.7% in 2026 and 4.1% for 2027.
ENERGY PRICE, AI RISKS
Participants at the IMF and World Bank meetings in Bangkok will be assessing a precarious outlook. The IMF forecasts are based on assumptions that the Strait of Hormuz will reopen in March 2027 with a broad return to pre-war shipping conditions occurring by October 2027. The IMF assumes an average oil price of $96 per barrel for 2026 and $87 in 2027.
But under an adverse scenario highlighted in the report, in which a worsening war pushes oil prices to $130 per barrel through the first quarter of 2027, growth would be reduced by 0.2 percentage point in 2026 and 0.5 percentage point in 2027. Inflation in 2027 would surge by another 1.1 percentage point to 5.2%.
AI is also a huge source of uncertainty, with major downside and upside risks, the IMF report said. Under a scenario of faster adoption of the technology and accelerated investment, global GDP could rise a further 0.6% by 2029, with the bulk of the benefits going to the US and China.
But if productivity gains from AI fail to materialize, prompting a sharp decline in investment, US GDP could fall by 0.8% directly, causing spillovers to Asian technology exporters with a total direct GDP impact of as much as 0.4% by 2028.
This shift would also trigger a sharp reduction in asset prices and tighter financial conditions that cause a major drop in consumption, particularly in the US, the IMF said. Higher global bond yields would further reduce activity, with a combined global output reduction of 1.1% by 2028, including a 1.8% drop in US output.
The IMF also warned that elevated public debt levels, particularly in advanced economies, increase the risk of sharply higher borrowing costs that can weigh on growth prospects. It urged governments to stop delaying action to rebuild fiscal buffers and articulate credible medium-term plans to bring debt back to sustainable levels — advice that IMF officials plan to push at the Bangkok meetings.

title: RBA minutes signal further rate hikes as inflation risks intensify
full_text:

Investing.com -- The Reserve Bank of Australia signalled further rate hikes remain possible as inflation risks intensify, minutes of its September meeting showed on Tuesday.
Policymakers were increasingly concerned that domestic capacity constraints and rising global costs could keep inflation elevated for longer than previously expected.
The minutes, released on Tuesday, showed that all members of the Monetary Policy Board supported raising the cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.60% at the September 28-29 meeting.
Members agreed that several upside risks to inflation identified in August had since materialised or intensified, while the economy continued to show resilience despite slowing demand.
The RBA said inflation remained too high and that earlier forecasts for inflation to return to the midpoint of its 2%-3% target range by late 2027 relied on a number of favourable developments that no longer appeared likely to materialise.
Further tightening remains on the table
The minutes struck a hawkish tone on the outlook for monetary policy. Members said timely action against additional cost pressures would help prevent inflation expectations from becoming less anchored, warning that waiting for further confirmation could prove costly after an extended period of above-target inflation.
The board also noted that the current cash rate might not be sufficiently restrictive if global neutral interest rates had risen. Tighter policy in other economies could also weaken the Australian dollar if domestic rates remained unchanged, potentially adding to inflationary pressures.
Policymakers did consider holding rates steady, citing risks that housing price declines, uncertainty linked to the Middle East conflict or the delayed effects of earlier monetary tightening could weigh more heavily on activity and employment.
However, they judged these risks insufficient to outweigh the need to contain inflation. The decision was unanimous, although the minutes acknowledged that achieving price stability would require accepting slower growth in demand and employment.
GDP growth beat expectations in the June quarter, supported by business investment rising more than 10% year on year, while household consumption slowed below trend and unemployment rose to 4.6% in August, with leading indicators pointing to near-term labour market stability.

title: Oil falls as Russia diesel supply prospects counter Gulf supply risks
full_text:
Wall Street kicks off key week of bank earnings and CPI data with a mixed session
By Anjana Anil and Trixie Yap
Oct 12 (Reuters) - Oil prices fell on Tuesday and were on track for their first decline in nearly a week, as traders assessed supply risks from attacks on Saudi Arabia while weighing the prospect of additional diesel supplies from Russia.
Brent crude futures fell $1.30, or 1.2%, to $105.35 a barrel by 0329 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures were down $1.25, or 1.3%, at $92.49 a barrel.
Both benchmarks climbed nearly $2 a barrel in the previous session, with Brent settling at its highest since September 15.
US President Donald Trump said Russia had agreed to supply diesel to global markets, and his administration temporarily lifted US sanctions on Russian fuel designed to deprive Moscow of revenue for its war on Ukraine.
Additional supplies could help alleviate tightness in global fuel markets, tempering some of the supply concerns that have supported crude prices recently.
However, "there is considerable scepticism over the Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire, particularly with reports that Russia has hit Ukrainian energy targets since Trump announced it," ING analysts said in a note.
Lawmakers from both parties in the US complained Trump’s agreement with Putin appears to violate US law barring imports of Russian energy until Moscow ends its aggression against Ukraine.
Concerns over the vulnerability of Gulf energy infrastructure and shipping lanes remained in focus after Iran-aligned Houthis struck Riyadh’s international airport over the weekend, while tanker attacks were reported near the Strait of Hormuz.
The incidents threatened to derail a recovery in Middle East supplies seen in September, and have reinforced fears of further disruptions along one of the world’s most important energy transit routes.
"Fresh diesel supply from Russia and steadier Saudi flows are offering some relief, yet the market still looks more worried about the risk of further hits to ships or pipelines in the Gulf than it is reassured by extra barrels," said Tim Waterer, chief analyst at KCM Trade.
"Until we see clearer signs of de-escalation, the path of least resistance still leans higher," he said.
Ministers of OPEC and non-OPEC Participating Countries in the Declaration of Cooperation said shipping and insurance costs have surged to unprecedented levels of over one-third of the commodity value, impeding efficient movement of crude oil and products.
OPEC has revised down its oil demand growth forecast for this year to 400,000 barrels per day from 1.4 million bpd at the start of the year, in line with developments throughout the year, Haitham Al Ghais, Secretary General of the organisation said on Monday.

title: IMF cites AI slowdown, spiking yields as looming global market risks
full_text:
Wall Street kicks off key week of bank earnings and CPI data with a mixed session
By Pete Schroeder
Oct 13 (Reuters) - The International Monetary Fund warned on Tuesday against "complacency" in global financial markets, citing risks from an artificial intelligence-driven selloff, rising government bond yields, or cyberattacks as potential threats facing still- resilient markets.
The body cautioned in its latest Global Financial Stability Report that should AI profits or investments wane, it could trigger a correction in related asset prices that could spill into broader markets. Such a selloff, as well as a spike in sovereign bond yields or a major cyberattack, were among "plausible near-term catalysts" that policymakers should monitor, the group wrote.
"These risks by themselves do not necessarily threaten financial stability but could become systemic...if they areamplified by underlying vulnerabilities," the group said in the semiannual report, adding that financial stability risks remain elevated.
The IMF said AI investments have so far helped offset economic drags from war in the Middle East and overall policy uncertainty. But it noted "growing evidence" that AI capabilities may not require as much investment, or the potential economic gains may not be as large as expected.
Should the momentum slow, the IMF noted growing leverage in the AI sector could exacerbate any shock by triggering forced selling and higher volatility. For example, hyperscalers now represent 10% of global investment-grade bond issuance, up from less than 1% in 2024.
"The consequences of an AI correction could be global," the IMF warned, as it called on policymakers to curb leverage use, including derivatives and margin loans, where it is "excessive."
RISING YIELDS
The IMF said bond market risks have worsened since its April report, as higher energy prices have driven government bond yields up. For one, policymakers may need to drive up monetary policy rates to tackle inflation, which in turn could worsen debt burdens for nations rolling over short-term debt. In addition, more price-sensitive investors could add upward pressure to yields, and market liquidity could suffer amid the more volatile environment.

In its World Economic Outlook, released early on Tuesday in Bangkok, the Fund projected regional growth of 2.3% this year. That is down from 2.5% growth in 2025 and from its July forecast of 2.4% growth for 2026. The IMF cut its 2027 forecast to 2.5% from 2.7%.
The regional downgrades come even as the Fund nudged up its world growth forecast for this year to 3.1% from July’s 3.0%, crediting rerouted energy supplies and AI-driven investment for the resilience of what it calls a split global economy.
The Middle East war has turned energy into a global inflation shock, with Brent crude about 45% above its prewar level. Higher fuel and power costs are squeezing households and businesses, while fears of persistent inflation have helped push global borrowing costs to multidecade highs.
In Latin America, the IMF said, the energy shock’s effect depends on whether gains for commodity exporters outweigh losses for energy importers and on how credible central banks’ inflation targets are, adding that "there is little offset from the technology upturn in most countries."
Of the three Latin American economies the IMF listed separately in its July World Economic Outlook update, Argentina took the deepest cut in its output estimate. The Fund now expects Argentine growth to slow to 2.1% this year from 4.5% in 2025, well below the 3.5% it forecast in July, and it lowered its 2027 forecast to 3.5% from 4.0%. The report shows inflation is forecast to fall to 32.5% this year from 41.9% in 2025.
Brazil’s forecasts fell to 2.2% for this year and 1.9% for 2027, from 2.4% and 2.2% in July, when the IMF had expected Brazilian growth to "remain resilient" this year. The Fund now expects growth to slow next year, citing still-restrictive monetary conditions aimed at bringing inflation back to target, the withdrawal of government fiscal support and global uncertainty.
Mexico moved the other way, with its 2026 forecast raised to 1.5% from 1.2%. The Fund previously linked Mexico’s expected pickup to less restrictive domestic policies. It now points to exports, including through AI supply chains, and to investment that is stabilizing as growth quickens next year. Even so, it trimmed Mexico’s 2027 forecast to 1.8% from 1.9% and said trade and other uncertainties would keep holding back activity.
The report’s tables show Chile’s growth slowing to 0.6% this year from 2.5%, Bolivia’s economy shrinking 3.0% after a 1.6% contraction in 2025, and Venezuelan inflation speeding up to 467.9% from 252.0%.
The IMF said risks remain tilted to the downside. It warned that market turmoil could hit emerging economies through higher government borrowing costs, pressure on their currencies and tighter local financial conditions.

title: Hedge funds are a top draw in Asia as investors look beyond bonds
full_text:
Wall Street kicks off key week of bank earnings and CPI data with a mixed session
By Summer Zhen and Tom Westbrook
HONG KONG, Oct 13 (Reuters) - Hedge funds are drawing in new fans and a rush of capital from Asia, as pensions, family offices and other investors look to alternative managers to help them navigate volatile debt markets and wobbly equities.
Private bankers and asset allocators told Reuters that Asian investors are increasingly seeking asset diversification compared to their usual allocations to equities and bonds.
The trend is the latest pressure point for traditional long-only managers, whose performances have come under scrutiny due to volatility in markets. It also raises questions on investors’ default risk-management strategy of the 60/40 allocation to stocks and fixed income.
Global hedge fund assets grew by a record for any quarter in the second quarter of 2026 when they rose $409 billion to $5.6 trillion, according to data from Hedge Fund Research (HFR).
At UBP, the share of hedge-fund-only mandates among its Asia-based discretionary portfolio management clients has more than tripled since end-2024, the Swiss private bank said, without providing any numbers.
"US Treasuries and government bonds have become a less reliable diversifier over the last few years," said Paras Gupta, head of discretionary portfolio management Asia at UBP, adding that this has widened the role hedge funds can play in portfolios.
Hedge fund performance has also held up relatively well, coinciding with a long rough patch in bond markets that has turned a safe asset supposed to hold its value into a loser in portfolios.
A global hedge fund index tracked by HFR gained 12.4% in 2025, a third consecutive positive year and the best performance since 2009. The index is up another 7% year-to-date.
Since the end of 2024, global stocks as measured by the MSCI world index have gained about 36% while the FTSE world government bond total return index has fallen 7%.
"We do want to bring in more on the alternative asset classes," said Rani Piputri, senior director of public investment at Danantara Investment Management, which is part of Indonesia’s sovereign wealth fund and is aiming for a 5% hedge fund exposure.
"Because we want to have a stable return with minimum drawdown."
NEW INVESTORS, NEW DRIVERS
Niall O’Sullivan, global chief investment officer at strategic adviser Marsh, said some institutional investors that did not use hedge funds before now want a roughly 10% exposure, especially to multi-strategy funds with low correlation to broader markets.
Interest has come from wealth managers, family offices and big investors including Japan’s defined-benefit pensions where bonds’ poor performance as a diversifier has been a particular concern, said Adeline Tan, head of investments at Marsh Asia.
Investors also think the extreme bifurcation — whether splitting markets between AI winners and losers or driven by geopolitical rifts — creates opportunities for long-short hedge funds to profit from price differences.
"Within tech, you have semiconductors outperforming software ... (the) US is outperforming the rest of the world," said Daryl Ho, senior investment strategist at DBS Bank.
Albert Yang, head of Alternative Investments for Asia at J.P. Morgan Private Bank, said hedge funds are increasingly being used as a long-term allocation to manage volatility, citing growing concerns about concentration risk in AI.
To be sure, performance and the flow of investment within the hedge fund industry are widely dispersed. Yang said the shift toward hedge fund exposure was not replacing traditional portfolios, but complementing them with new strategies and resilience.
Multi-strategy, macro and quantitative managers that are nimble and can generate returns independent of equity market direction have been among the biggest beneficiaries.
Acadian Asset Management, a $233 billion systematic fund that collects data on tens of thousands of companies and runs strategies that aim to modestly but consistently outperform equity indexes, has seen its assets in Asia quadruple in four years.
"It’s been 20 years since we think we’ve seen this level of interest," said Kelly Young, Acadian’s chief executive officer.

title: Growing debt burden poses significant risk to developing nations, G24 chair says
full_text:
Wall Street kicks off key week of bank earnings and CPI data with a mixed session
By Rae Wee
BANGKOK, Oct 13 (Reuters) - The debt vulnerabilities of many developing economies are a "major barrier" to inclusive growth, the chair of the Group of 24 nations said on Tuesday, warning their governments were increasingly contending with mounting debt burdens.
Speaking to reporters at the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank in Bangkok, Taiwo Oyedele said estimates showed developing nations were paying roughly $500 billion more for their debt than developed countries, as economies grapple with growing fiscal deficits.
"What we have seen by members of the G24 and across particularly the developing countries such as those in Africa, is an increasing body of not just high debts, but high costs of debts," said Oyedele, who is also Nigeria’s minister of finance and coordinating minister of the economy.
Heavily indebted developing countries have come under immense pressure this year, strained by supply shocks from the ongoing war in the Middle East, rising food prices triggered by a "super El Niño" and surging borrowing costs.
"These developments impact emerging markets and developing economies’ progress towards achieving inclusive and job-rich economic transformation," Oyedele said.
PUSH FOR GREATER SUPPORT
Members of the G24, a bloc of emerging and developing market nations, urged the IMF and World Bank to provide more accessible and affordable concessional financing to vulnerable countries in the near-term, as they worked to mobilise private capital and reduce public spending.
"Debt is something that restrains growth, because countries then do not have enough resources to finance further growth, or they are spending most of their resources just paying off the debt," said Iyabo Masha, director of the G24 secretariat.
However, she said that recent improvements to the sovereign debt architecture should help countries resolve debt crises more quickly.
Citing Senegal as an example, Masha said the country was "quite close" to a final resolution with its creditors.
Reuters reported last week the West African nation was aiming for an agreement in principle with its official lenders and bondholders by December, two years after the emergence of misreported debt that analysts estimated at $13 billion.
Beyond debt challenges, developing economies also risk being left behind in the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence.
The IMF earlier on Tuesday trimmed its growth forecasts for Latin America and the Caribbean for this year and next, saying most of the region was getting little lift from the AI boom that has helped other economies absorb the energy shock from the Middle East war.
"It is a concern that (AI) will widen the digital divide," Masha told Reuters on the sidelines of the G24 press conference.
"For the countries that have not yet reached certain levels of development, they will be starting from scratch. The role of AI, they would not benefit much for now.
"Maybe if they have good access to electricity, they may be able to have a data centre investment and all that. But without that, it would take a while for them to start benefiting."
